summaries.example: Imagine you see a red ball. Chisholm would ask: What makes it reasonable for you to believe the ball is red? Your seeing, touching, and remembering may support the belief. But if you know you took a drug that causes false pictures, that wider situation may defeat the usual support.
summaries.summary: Roderick Chisholm was an influential American philosopher who worked on knowledge, persons, action, events, language, and ethics. He liked to begin with puzzles and familiar judgments. He then introduced a few basic ideas and used them to build systems of definitions and principles. In epistemology, he tried to explain how ordinary knowledge is possible without accepting skepticism. He described ways that beliefs about our minds, senses, memories, and connected evidence might support knowledge. In metaphysics, he defended the importance of persons as genuine beings and explored how identity survives change. He also developed a view of free action involving a person’s own causal contribution. His work examined thoughts about nonexistent objects, possible worlds, events, and parts. In ethics, he used the idea of requirement to explain value, obligation, and situations in which good or bad can be weakened by a larger situation. Chisholm changed details of his theories many times, so the entry presents a sketch rather than one final answer.
key_ideas: Chisholm began with questions and everyday beliefs, then built careful definitions and principles.
He thought we really do know many ordinary things, such as facts about the world and the past.
He argued that persons are more than temporary collections of body parts or experiences.
He connected free action with a person helping to cause an action.
He kept revising his views when students and other philosophers found problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chisholm shows how philosophy can connect ordinary experiences with very difficult questions. His work asks how we know, what makes a person the same person over time, whether choices can be free, and how moral duties work. It also models a useful habit: listen carefully to objections and improve an idea instead of protecting it unchanged.

important_terms.definition: The study of what knowledge is and how people can know things.
A careful puzzle or difficulty that a theory should try to explain.
A reason for a belief that can be overcome by a stronger reason or special situation.
The idea that a person can sometimes choose and act in a way not forced by earlier events.
The idea that thoughts are about things, even things that may not exist, such as a unicorn.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a belief reasonable rather than just a guess?
If a ship gets all new parts, is it still the same ship?
Can someone be responsible if everything about the action was already forced?
Can you think about something that does not exist?

summaries.example: Suppose you believe there is a doorknob in front of you. Your current visual experience may make that belief reasonable. Memories and other sensory evidence may support it further. But if you know you are hallucinating, that larger context can defeat the ordinary evidence. This illustrates Chisholm’s attempt to connect foundational self-knowledge with knowledge of the external world while allowing evidence to be overridden.
summaries.summary: Roderick Chisholm developed a broad philosophical system spanning epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of mind and language, free will, logic, and ethics. His characteristic procedure was systematic: identify puzzles and pre-theoretical judgments, select a small number of primitive notions, and derive definitions and principles from them. In epistemology, he accepted common-sense knowledge of the external world, memory, and some necessary truths, while asking how such knowledge is possible. He treated direct evidence about one’s current states as foundational, then used principles involving perception, memory, confirmation, and coherent support to explain further knowledge. He was a particularist in the problem of the criterion and an internalist about justification, opposing theories that make justification depend essentially on causal reliability or empirical science. In metaphysics, he argued that persons are genuine persisting substances, not merely bundles of perceptions or bodies whose identity changes with every replaced part. His discussions of events and states of affairs repeatedly reduced or pruned the categories in his ontology, eventually removing times and recurring states from a later, sparser account. His work on intentionality developed versions of Brentano’s idea that psychological description has a distinctive aboutness. His paradoxes about possible worlds and changing parts challenged easy accounts of identity. In action theory, he defended agent causation and an indeterministic form of libertarianism. In ethics, he analyzed intrinsic value through fitting preference and made requirement central to obligation, including conditional and overridden duties. key_ideas: Chisholm’s method moved from pre-theoretical data and puzzles to primitive concepts, definitions, and principles.
His epistemology was anti-skeptical and particularist: it began from many things we ordinarily take ourselves to know, while acknowledging the problem of the criterion.
He combined foundationalist and coherentist elements: direct evidence could support further beliefs, while mutually supporting acceptable beliefs could raise their epistemic status.
His account of persons treated them as genuine substances and resisted identifying persons simply with bodies or bundles of perceptions.
His libertarian account of freedom appealed to agent causation and indeterminism: a free action is not fixed by sufficient earlier event conditions.
His ethics used requirement to analyze intrinsic value, prima facie obligation, overridden obligation, and conditional duties.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chisholm’s philosophy matters because it links formal precision with questions people recognize: how evidence supports belief, what makes someone the same person, whether responsibility requires genuine alternatives, and how obligations change when circumstances change. His arguments also helped shape later debates about internalism, personal identity, intentionality, possible worlds, deontic logic, and value. Just as important, his willingness to revise definitions illustrates philosophy as an ongoing inquiry rather than a finished collection of doctrines.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of knowledge, justification, evidence, and the standards for knowing.
A basic concept treated as a starting point rather than defined through simpler concepts.
The view that some knowledge is directly justified and can support further, less direct knowledge.
The view that justification depends on what is available through reflection on one’s conscious state, rather than on outside causal or reliability facts.
A kind of causation in which an agent, not only an event, contributes to what happens.
The view that a thing has its parts essentially and cannot remain that very thing after losing them.
The aboutness of mental states or sentences, including thought about things that may not exist.
A relation in which what happens makes something required, though that requirement may later be overridden.

questions_to_think_about: Can a theory of knowledge begin with examples of what we know without assuming the very standard it is trying to discover?
Does the Ship of Theseus show that identity is conventional, or that ordinary objects are less fundamental than persons or basic substances?
Would agent causation explain freedom, or does it merely add another unexplained source of action?
Can a statement about probability or comparison be intentional even when it does not describe a mental state?
How should a logic represent an obligation that depends on having failed an earlier obligation?

summaries.example: A student sees a strange shape in a dim room and believes it is a backpack. The belief is supported by sight and by remembering that a backpack was left there. But if the student also knows the room has a projector making misleading shapes, that extra fact may defeat the evidence. Chisholm’s ideas help us ask how evidence normally supports belief and when a wider situation changes its force.
summaries.summary: Roderick Chisholm was a major American philosopher whose work covered knowledge, reality, persons, action, intentionality, logic, and ethics. He used a recognizable method. He began with puzzles and judgments that seemed reasonable before theory, introduced a few basic concepts, and then built a network of definitions and principles. In epistemology, he started from the idea that people do know many ordinary things. He asked how knowledge of the outside world, the past, and necessary truths could be possible. His principles connected self-awareness, perception, memory, confirmation, and groups of mutually supporting beliefs. Chisholm was a particularist in the problem of the criterion: he began from some cases of knowledge rather than first finding a general test. He also defended internalism, according to which justification should be available through reflection on one’s conscious state. In metaphysics, he treated persons as genuine objects and questioned theories that reduce a person to a bundle of experiences or a body. His discussions of identity used changing ships and possible worlds to show that ordinary ideas about sameness can produce difficult puzzles. He developed an account of free action involving agent causation, indeterminism, and what is directly or indirectly within a person’s power. He also proposed different systems for understanding events and states of affairs, later moving toward a more economical ontology. In philosophy of mind and language, he refined Brentano-inspired accounts of intentionality. In ethics, he made requirement central to intrinsic value and obligation, including duties that arise after wrongdoing and duties that can be defeated by new circumstances. key_ideas: Chisholm built theories from puzzles, familiar judgments, basic ideas, definitions, and principles.
He defended common-sense knowledge while admitting that explaining its standards creates a difficult circular-looking problem.
His theory of knowledge included both foundational support and networks of mutually supporting beliefs.
He argued that personal identity should not be reduced simply to a body or a collection of changing experiences.
His account of freedom distinguished what is logically possible or imaginable from what is genuinely within an agent’s power.
He explored how moral duties can depend on circumstances, be overridden, and differ from actions that are especially good but not required.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chisholm’s work matters because it shows how one philosopher tried to connect everyday certainty with highly abstract theory. His questions remain useful for thinking about evidence, personal identity, freedom, mental content, and moral responsibility. His method also offers a lesson in intellectual work: precise definitions can clarify a debate, but counterexamples may require those definitions to be revised.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge: what we know, how beliefs are supported, and what counts as a good reason.
A starting idea that is not explained using simpler ideas in the theory.
A reason or piece of evidence that supports a belief but can be overridden by stronger information.
The problem of deciding whether to begin with examples of knowledge or with a rule for recognizing knowledge.
The view that justification can be determined by reflection on a person’s conscious mental state.
A view of persons as real beings that have thoughts, feelings, bodies, and actions.
A form of causation in which a person helps bring about an event, not merely one event causing another.
The idea that a thought or sentence can be about something, even if that thing does not exist.

questions_to_think_about: If two people have the same conscious experiences, must they be justified in believing the same things?
When a ship’s boards are gradually replaced, what kind of sameness might remain?
Is an action free only when it was not determined by earlier events?
Why might thinking about a unicorn be different from seeing or touching a unicorn?
Can an obligation to apologize exist even though a morally perfect person would never have needed to apologize?
